sections.subtitle: The Spanish Alphabet
sections.content: Spanish uses the Latin alphabet with 27 letters. It includes all English letters plus 'ñ'. The letters 'k' and 'w' are rare and mostly appear in foreign words.

sections.subtitle: Vowels (a, e, i, o, u)
sections.content: Spanish vowels are always pronounced the same way: 'a' like in 'father', 'e' like in 'pet', 'i' like in 'machine', 'o' like in 'go', 'u' like in 'rule'. There are no silent vowels.

sections.subtitle: Key Consonants
sections.content: H is always silent. J sounds like a strong 'h'. LL sounds like 'y'. Ñ sounds like 'ny' (as in 'canyon'). V and B sound identical. R is rolled when at the start or doubled (rr). G before e/i sounds like 'h', otherwise like 'g' in 'go'.

sections.subtitle: Accent Marks (´)
sections.content: Accent marks show which syllable to stress. Words ending in vowel, n, or s stress the second-to-last syllable by default. Words ending in other consonants stress the last syllable. Accent marks override these rules.

sections.subtitle: Special Sound: Ñ
sections.content: The letter ñ (called 'eñe') is unique to Spanish. It represents a 'ny' sound as in 'canyon' or 'onion'. Examples: año (year), niño (child), español (Spanish).

questions.question: Which letter is always silent in Spanish?
questions.hint: This letter appears in words like 'hola' and 'hacer' but makes no sound at all.

questions.question: How is the letter 'j' pronounced in Spanish?
questions.hint: The Spanish 'j' makes a throaty sound similar to the 'ch' in the Scottish 'loch' or German 'Bach'.

questions.question: Which two letters sound identical in Spanish?
questions.hint: Native Spanish speakers often have trouble distinguishing these letters when spelling aloud.

questions.question: What sound does 'll' make in most Spanish dialects?
questions.hint: In words like 'llamar' (to call) or 'calle' (street), this makes a 'y' sound.

questions.question: How do you pronounce 'ñ'?
questions.hint: Think of English words 'onion' or 'canyon' - that 'ny' sound is what 'ñ' represents.

questions.question: Spanish vowels are...
questions.hint: Unlike English, Spanish vowels have one consistent sound each. This makes pronunciation predictable.

questions.question: When is the letter 'r' rolled in Spanish?

answers.text: At the start of a word or when doubled (rr)
Only at the end of words
Never - it's always a soft tap

questions.hint: Compare 'pero' (but) with a soft tap, versus 'perro' (dog) with a strong roll.

questions.question: What do accent marks (´) indicate in Spanish?
questions.hint: Accent marks help you know WHERE to put emphasis when speaking. Example: 'papá' (dad) vs 'papa' (potato).

questions.question: How many letters are in the Spanish alphabet?
questions.hint: Spanish has all the English letters plus one special letter: ñ.

questions.question: Which letters are rare in Spanish?

answers.text: k and w (mostly in foreign words)

questions.hint: These two letters are uncommon because they mainly appear in borrowed words from other languages.

questions.question: How is the vowel 'a' pronounced in Spanish?
questions.hint: Spanish 'a' has an open sound, similar to the 'a' in the English word 'father'.

questions.question: How is the vowel 'i' pronounced in Spanish?
questions.hint: Spanish 'i' sounds like the long 'e' sound in English, as in 'see' or 'machine'.

questions.question: How is the vowel 'u' pronounced in Spanish?
questions.hint: Spanish 'u' has the 'oo' sound, like in the English words 'rule' or 'food'.

questions.question: How is 'g' pronounced before 'e' or 'i'?
questions.hint: Before 'e' or 'i', 'g' sounds like Spanish 'j' - a throaty 'h'. Example: 'gente' (people).

questions.question: How is 'g' pronounced before 'a', 'o', or 'u'?
questions.hint: Before 'a', 'o', or 'u', 'g' has its hard sound. Example: 'gato' (cat), 'gusto' (pleasure).

questions.question: Where is stress placed by default in words ending in vowel, 'n', or 's'?
questions.hint: Without an accent mark, words like 'casa', 'hablan', and 'libros' stress the second-to-last syllable.

questions.question: Where is stress placed by default in words ending in consonants (except 'n' or 's')?
questions.hint: Words ending in consonants like 'l', 'd', 'r', 'z' stress the last syllable. Example: 'papel', 'ciudad'.

questions.question: What does an accent mark do to stress rules?
questions.hint: Accent marks show exceptions. 'Café' has an accent because it breaks the default rule (should stress 'ca').

questions.question: Are there ever silent vowels in Spanish?

answers.text: No - all vowels are always pronounced
Vowels at the end are silent

questions.hint: Unlike English, every vowel in Spanish is pronounced. No silent vowels exist.

questions.question: What's the difference between 'pero' and 'perro'?

answers.text: 'pero' has a soft tap 'r', 'perro' has a rolled 'rr'

questions.hint: 'pero' (but) = soft tap. 'perro' (dog) = strong rolled sound. The 'r' vs 'rr' changes meaning!
